rows.label: Chart data: revenue and EBITDA — paragraph 1

limitations: Produced in a host session and accepted by the CP-OS check.
Literal checked analytical handoff, not native contract acceptance; source qualifications and gaps remain.

- Debt maturities by year at 2026-09-30: no quarterly report prints a schedule, so the ladder is drawn at 2025-12-31, before the Virginia 3 refinancing, the securitization amendment and the 2035 notes; this restricts the maturity wall to the year-end view and the printed current portion at 2026-09-30. Severity: High. Action: obtain the issuer's schedule at the latest date or derive it, labelled derived, from instrument principal and stated maturities. - Debt stack: Real Estate Mortgages, Financing Lease Liabilities and Other (carrying USD 818.241 million) is left out of the stack because no source states the rank of the pool, and the stack therefore adds to less than total debt; this restricts the cumulative leverage in the stack to the instruments whose rank is stated. Severity: Medium. Action: obtain the component ranking and security. - Lease payments and purchase commitments by year at 2026-09-30: the quarterly reports print lease balances and one new finance lease but no payment schedule; the annual report schedule is at 2025-12-31. This restricts claims outside debt to year-end schedules and balances at the latest date. Severity: Medium. Action: obtain the schedule at the latest date. - Covenant perimeter: the subsidiaries designated as Unrestricted Subsidiaries are not named in the four filings, and the covenant ratios use EBITDAR and EBITDA definitions that differ from Adjusted EBITDA; this restricts any reconciliation of reported covenant ratios to the consolidated statements. Severity: Medium. Action: obtain the designation list and the covenant definitions from the executed documents. - Gross profit for every period: the issuer prints no gross profit and its cost of sales excludes depreciation and amortization, so none is stated; this restricts gross margin analysis. Severity: Low. Action: none needed for leverage and coverage. - Restructuring and other transformation for Q1 2026, H1 2026, Q3 2026 and 9M 2026: the quarterly statements print a dash, recorded as missing and not as zero; this restricts the exceptional-item total for 2026 to the lines that are stated. Severity: Low. Action: none needed, since Adjusted EBITDA and reported EBITDA are built from other lines. - Total Liabilities for every balance sheet date: the issuer prints no total liabilities line, so the figure is calculated from the printed liability lines; this restricts nothing, since the balance sheet identity holds at every date. Severity: Low. Action: none. - Undrawn committed facilities at 2024-12-31: the annual report states revolver availability at 2025-12-31 only, so the figure is missing for the earlier year; this restricts the liquidity comparison to the later four dates. Severity: Low. Action: none needed for the latest date. - Debt stack: the 2035 senior notes are shown as unsecured because the Q3 report classes them with the other Parent Notes, which the annual report describes as effectively subordinated to secured debt; the 2035 indenture itself is not in the sources. Severity: Low. Action: confirm against the indenture. - Cash flow lines with a dash or no printed figure are recorded as missing and not as zero: Cash paid for acquisitions, net of cash acquired (Q1 2026, H1 2026); Net proceeds from sale of senior notes (Q1 2025, H1 2025, Q1 2026); Equity contributions from noncontrolling interests (Q1 2025, H1 2025, 9M 2025, Q1 2026). This restricts those lines to the periods in which they are stated; the three activity totals and the cash roll-forward are unaffected. Severity: Low. Action: none needed. - Discrete second-quarter and third-quarter 2026 cash flows: each quarterly report prints year-to-date cash flows only, so single-quarter cash flow figures are not stated; this restricts quarterly free cash flow to differences of printed totals. Severity: Low. Action: label any single-quarter cash flow as derived. - Q4 2025 stand-alone figures: no fourth-quarter report or release was supplied, so the quarter is not stated; it would be the 2025 year less nine months 2025, both printed. This restricts any fourth-quarter comparison to a derived figure. Severity: Low. Action: label derived figures. - Debt instrument terms: the Q3 report restates amounts but not the maturity dates, margins, commitments and amortisation of the Term Loans, the project loans and the UK facility, which are taken from the annual report at 2025-12-31; any amendment after that date other than the Virginia 3 refinancing, the Virginia 9 agreement and the securitization amendment is not reflected. Severity: Low. Action: confirm at the next report. - Foreign currency debt: the euro notes, the Australian dollar term loan and the sterling facility are printed in US dollars at 2026-09-30, so their amounts in the currency of denomination at that date are not stated (the annual report states them at 2025-12-31); no exchange rate is used. Severity: Low. Action: none needed for carrying values. - Rate basis of the Virginia 3 Term Loans due 2031, the benchmark and margin of the receivables securitization, and the scheduled amortisation of the project loans: not stated in the sources read; this restricts the floating-rate share of debt to the instruments whose rate basis is stated. Severity: Low. Action: obtain the loan terms. - Post-balance-sheet effect of the dividend declared on 2026-11-05: the total amount is not stated (only 0.993 USD per share, record date 2026-12-15 and payment date 2027-01-06), so the effect on net debt, pro forma net debt and pro forma net leverage is not stated; the figure is not worked out here. Severity: Low. Action: state the amount when the issuer discloses the total. - Operating KPIs: prior-year organic revenue growth, and data center leasing in the prior-year quarter and nine months, are not stated in the sources read; this restricts the dashboard to the current-year values for those rows. Severity: Low. Action: none needed.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Dividend policy is the clearest creditor-adverse behaviour, because payouts rise while investment outruns operating cash flow. facts.label: Bottom line
facts.text: Iron Mountain's fundamental credit is adequate but leverage-dependent: a contracted, diversified records base and a growing data center book support cash flow, yet net debt of 6.87x reported EBITDA, thin interest cover and negative free cash flow make credit quality depend on EBITDA outgrowing debt. Net debt over reported EBITDA fell from 7.88x at the end of 2025 to 6.87x at 30 September 2026 because earnings grew while debt rose; the dividend declared on 5 November 2026 is not reflected, and its pro forma effect on net debt is not established. Basis: calculation CAL-1; calculation CAL-2; Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 24

Basis: calculation CAL-41; calculation CAL-42; calculation CAL-14; Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1)

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: The business profile is stronger than the financial profile, and the gap between them is the credit. Global RIM Business produced 71.71% of nine-month revenue, storage rental was 56.73% of revenue, no customer exceeds about 3% of revenue and storage contracts run one to five years, so the cash base is recurring and diversified. Against that, net debt of 6.87x reported EBITDA and cash interest cover of 2.83x mean that the franchise's stability is already largely spent servicing debt: cash interest took 31.68% of last-twelve-months Adjusted EBITDA. Basis: calculation CAL-42; calculation CAL-44; calculation CAL-23; calculation CAL-7; 10-K_2025-12-31_irm-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-K_2025-12-31_irm-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 11; Business & governance (CP-1A); Financial foundation (CP-1)

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Deleveraging is real but earnings-led, and it overstates the operating gain. Net debt over reported EBITDA fell 1.01x in nine months while carrying-value debt rose USD 1,540.24 million and last-twelve-months reported EBITDA rose USD 524.13 million; on Adjusted EBITDA, which adds back items that did not recur, net leverage eased only 0.16x to 6.16x. The improvement therefore reflects earnings already delivered, not debt repaid, and the dividend declared on 5 November 2026 is not reflected in these ratios, its pro forma effect on net debt not being established. Basis: calculation CAL-5; calculation CAL-6; calculation CAL-10; calculation CAL-11; calculation CAL-3; Financial foundation (CP-1)

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: The cash shortfall is a growth choice, not an operating failure, which is the best argument that the credit can stabilise. In the nine months to 30 September 2026 operating cash flow less accrual-basis recurring capital expenditure was USD 1,085.34 million, and after dividends paid of USD 790.00 million it was still USD 295.34 million, so maintenance and the payout were self-funded; growth investment was 93.07% of capital spending and is what pushes free cash flow after capital expenditure to a shortfall of USD 536.82 million over the last twelve months. The weakness is that the dividend per share was raised 14.93% on 5 November 2026 while growth spending continues, which erodes that surplus. Basis: calculation CAL-18; calculation CAL-19; calculation CAL-20; calculation CAL-9; calculation CAL-51; calculation CAL-52; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 45; Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A)

facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against the cautious reading is that the shortfall is discretionary and the business is outgrowing its debt: growth investment is 93.07% of capital spending, operating cash flow covers maintenance and the dividend with USD 295.34 million to spare, covenant leverage of 4.8x sits 2.2x inside its 7.0x maximum and fixed charge coverage of 2.5x sits 1.0x above its 1.5x minimum, the debt terms carry no rating trigger, and the company has extended maturities at par in both bond markets. facts.text: Iron Mountain is a listed holding company with no sponsor, parent or controlling holder named; the charter caps any holder at 9.8% and the board sets dividends in its sole discretion, so creditors depend on governance and covenants rather than on a sponsor. facts.text: Margins are resilient on the consolidated measure and uneven underneath. facts.label: Competitive forces
facts.text: Competitive pressure is moderate in records and higher in data centers and asset lifecycle management. In records most competitors operate in one market or region, so Iron Mountain's global scale and chain-of-custody record are a barrier that supports pricing; in data centers it competes with many developers on power availability, security, location, connectivity and rent, and in asset lifecycle management it competes with hyperscalers and corporate clients that process their own assets. New entrants face high capital and power barriers in data centers and trust barriers in records, which protects existing cash flows but also means the company must keep spending to hold its position. facts.label: Competitive forces
facts.text: Substitutes and buyers are the main sources of pressure on the base business: customers who adopt non-paper storage or retain records for less time shrink the physical volume and shift revenue from predictable storage to volatile service, and some large-customer contracts carry no limit on liability. Supplier power is real in data centers, where power, construction contractors and permits drive cost and timing, and in asset lifecycle management, where component buyers are concentrated; the credit consequence is cost and delay risk on the capacity that debt is funding. facts.label: Macro, regulatory and technology factors
facts.text: Interest rates, currency and tax rules matter to credit; political and social factors do not appear to be primary drivers in the supplied documents. Floating-rate debt and thin cover make rate changes material, 22.51% of FY2025 revenue arises outside the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada with euro and sterling debt acting as a partial natural hedge, a 10% depreciation of functional currencies would reduce equity by USD 374.7 million, and the real estate investment trust rules require a 90% distribution of taxable income, while a 2026 change in the limit on assets held in taxable subsidiaries and the global minimum tax are not expected to have a material effect. Digitisation and artificial intelligence cut both ways: they reduce physical record activity but support digital solutions. facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: The primary downside path starts with a delay or shortfall in data center leasing or energizing while construction commitments continue, and turns into a leverage and refinancing problem rather than an immediate liquidity one. Revenue growth in the data center segment, now 39.61%, would slow first; because facility costs and the debt service on completed capacity would continue while rent was delayed, the segment margin of 53.60% would fall, and service and asset lifecycle management revenue would add to the pressure if component prices or activity weakened. As an arithmetic sensitivity and not a forecast, a 10% fall in last-twelve-months reported EBITDA with net debt and interest unchanged lifts net debt over reported EBITDA from 6.87x to 7.63x and cuts cash interest cover from 2.83x to 2.55x, close to the year-end 2025 levels of 7.88x and 2.50x, or to 6.84x and 2.84x on Adjusted EBITDA; a 1% rise in rates on uncovered floating-rate debt would add about USD 37.29 million of annual interest, 4.08% of cash interest, against the company's own year-end 2025 sensitivity of USD 41.9 million of net income for a 1% rise on 22.0% variable-rate debt. facts.label: Overall credit view
facts.text: Overall, Iron Mountain presents an adequate business profile supported by a contracted, diversified records base and long-dated data center leases, but credit quality is constrained by net debt of 6.87x reported EBITDA, a free cash flow shortfall of USD 536.82 million over the last twelve months and claims that rank ahead of parent noteholders. Cash-flow durability appears adequate because maintenance spending and the dividend are self-funded and covenants have headroom, and refinancing capacity is likely to depend on continued EBITDA growth, the revolver and open bond markets, with about 14.08% of year-end 2025 principal due in 2027. The primary downside path is a data center slowdown that leaves debt-funded capacity idle while the payout keeps rising. Further analysis would require the maturity schedule after the 2026 refinancings, tenant concentration, the executed debt documents and a rating, and the dividend declared on 5 November 2026 is not reflected in the leverage figures, its pro forma effect on net debt not being established. The top risk is leverage that stays near its current level because EBITDA growth stalls. Basis: calculation CAL-1; calculation CAL-9; calculation CAL-15; calculation CAL-19; Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); Source readiness (CP-0)

## Findings
### Bottom line

Leverage is high but easing: net debt was 6.87x last-twelve-months reported EBITDA at 30 September 2026, down from 7.88x at the end of 2025, so creditors depend on continued EBITDA growth to keep refinancing risk contained. Reported EBITDA covered cash interest 2.83x over the same twelve months, or 3.16x on the issuer's Adjusted EBITDA.
Basis: calculation CAL-33; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2–4; 10-K_2025-12-31_irm-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 96–99

Liquidity at 30 September 2026 was cash of USD 188.16 million plus USD 2.22 billion of undrawn revolver, against USD 1.23 billion of debt due within a year, while capital spending still exceeds operating cash flow. The quarterly reports print no year-by-year maturity schedule, so the wall at that date is not established.

Basis: calculation CAL-35; calculation CAL-36; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 20; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 6–7; 10-K_2025-12-31_irm-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 98–99

### Leverage and coverage

Net debt over last-twelve-months reported EBITDA fell from 7.88x at the end of 2025 to 6.87x at 30 September 2026. The improvement came from EBITDA growth, not repayment: carrying-value debt rose by USD 1,540.243 million over the nine months while last-twelve-months reported EBITDA rose by USD 524.128 million.
Basis: calculation CAL-30; calculation CAL-31; calculation CAL-33; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2–4

Part of the reported gain is relief from items that did not recur: the issuer booked USD 152.432 million of restructuring and other transformation in the first nine months of 2025 and prints a dash for it in 2026, and other expense (income), net fell from USD 106.379 million to USD 32.910 million. On the issuer's Adjusted EBITDA, which adds those items back, net leverage eased by only 0.16x against 1.01x on reported EBITDA, so the headline deleveraging overstates the operating improvement.
Basis: calculation CAL-34; calculation CAL-33; calculation CAL-32; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 3–4; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 32

The strongest contrary evidence is operating momentum and covenant room: Adjusted EBITDA rose from USD 660.379 million in the third quarter of 2025 to USD 747.958 million in the third quarter of 2026, and the leverage ratio the issuer reports under its Credit Agreement sits inside its limit. That reading would win if reported EBITDA keeps converging on Adjusted EBITDA as restructuring ends, narrowing the gap from USD 508.992 million in FY2025 to USD 299.106 million in the last twelve months. Interest cover moved the same way, from 2.50x to 2.83x on reported EBITDA, but remains thin for a borrower whose capital spending exceeds its operating cash flow.
Basis: calculation CAL-39; calculation CAL-40; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 32; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 50
### Cash flow and funding

Capital expenditure exceeds operating cash flow, so growth is funded externally. In FY2025 operating cash flow of USD 1,339.999 million fell USD 931.629 million short of capital expenditure of USD 2,271.628 million, before dividends of USD 919.388 million. Over the last twelve months to 30 September 2026 the shortfall narrowed to USD 536.818 million, and the issuer expects total capital expenditure of about USD 2,200.0 million in 2026, of which about USD 2,050.0 million is growth investment.

The mechanism is data center construction financed by project debt, noncontrolling-interest equity (USD 95.168 million contributed in the nine months to 30 September 2026) and the revolver, which keeps total debt rising even as the ratio falls. The credit implication is that leverage stays sensitive to how fast leased capacity converts to EBITDA and to the cost and availability of refinancing.
### Liquidity and maturities

Cash of USD 188.160 million and undrawn revolver availability of USD 2,218.218 million at 30 September 2026 compare with debt due within twelve months of USD 1,232.903 million, up from USD 216.074 million at the year end. The annual report lists USD 2,330.763 million due in 2027 and USD 1,663.693 million in 2028 at the year end, so the near-term wall is front-loaded and the 2027 notes are among the next refinancing tests; the quarterly report does not itemise the current portion or print a schedule at 30 September 2026.

The availability figure is the issuer's maximum under its Credit Agreement tests and the compliance statement in the quarterly report applies to those tests, so liquidity depends on the revolver staying available as leverage moves. The filings state that the covenants contain no rating trigger.
### Data quality and definitions

Reported EBITDA is derived because the issuer states only an adjusted measure, and the covenant ratios use further definitions that are not directly comparable with either. Debt is carrying value; principal is USD 124.224 million higher at 30 September 2026. Operating lease liabilities of USD 2,518.768 million sit outside debt, while financing lease liabilities are inside it. Deferred revenue of USD 378.117 million is non-debt funding float, down from USD 402.091 million at the year end.
Basis: calculation CAL-38; calculation CAL-41; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 50

Segment revenue and Adjusted EBITDA add to the consolidated figures in all six columns of the segment schedule, the instrument carrying values add to Total Debt of USD 17.97 billion, and the FY2025 bridge reconciles reported EBITDA to Adjusted EBITDA exactly.

Basis: calculation CAL-37; calculation CAL-29; 10-K_2025-12-31_irm-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 164–166; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 25–26; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 46–47

The material gaps are the missing maturity and lease payment schedules at the latest date and the unnamed Unrestricted Subsidiaries, which restrict the maturity wall and any covenant reconciliation; the figures above are otherwise tied to the statements, and the balance sheet and cash flow identities hold in every column.

## Gaps

- Debt maturities by year at 2026-09-30: no quarterly report prints a schedule, so the ladder is drawn at 2025-12-31, before the Virginia 3 refinancing, the securitization amendment and the 2035 notes; this restricts the maturity wall to the year-end view and the printed current portion at 2026-09-30. Severity: High. Action: obtain the issuer's schedule at the latest date or derive it, labelled derived, from instrument principal and stated maturities.

- Debt stack: Real Estate Mortgages, Financing Lease Liabilities and Other (carrying USD 818.241 million) is left out of the stack because no source states the rank of the pool, and the stack therefore adds to less than total debt; this restricts the cumulative leverage in the stack to the instruments whose rank is stated. Severity: Medium. Action: obtain the component ranking and security.

- Lease payments and purchase commitments by year at 2026-09-30: the quarterly reports print lease balances and one new finance lease but no payment schedule; the annual report schedule is at 2025-12-31. This restricts claims outside debt to year-end schedules and balances at the latest date. Severity: Medium. Action: obtain the schedule at the latest date.

- Covenant perimeter: the subsidiaries designated as Unrestricted Subsidiaries are not named in the four filings, and the covenant ratios use EBITDAR and EBITDA definitions that differ from Adjusted EBITDA; this restricts any reconciliation of reported covenant ratios to the consolidated statements. Severity: Medium. Action: obtain the designation list and the covenant definitions from the executed documents.

- Gross profit for every period: the issuer prints no gross profit and its cost of sales excludes depreciation and amortization, so none is stated; this restricts gross margin analysis. Severity: Low. Action: none needed for leverage and coverage.

- Restructuring and other transformation for Q1 2026, H1 2026, Q3 2026 and 9M 2026: the quarterly statements print a dash, recorded as missing and not as zero; this restricts the exceptional-item total for 2026 to the lines that are stated. Severity: Low. Action: none needed, since Adjusted EBITDA and reported EBITDA are built from other lines.

- Total Liabilities for every balance sheet date: the issuer prints no total liabilities line, so the figure is calculated from the printed liability lines; this restricts nothing, since the balance sheet identity holds at every date. Severity: Low. Action: none.

- Undrawn committed facilities at 2024-12-31: the annual report states revolver availability at 2025-12-31 only, so the figure is missing for the earlier year; this restricts the liquidity comparison to the later four dates. Severity: Low. Action: none needed for the latest date.

- Debt stack: the 2035 senior notes are shown as unsecured because the Q3 report classes them with the other Parent Notes, which the annual report describes as effectively subordinated to secured debt; the 2035 indenture itself is not in the sources. Severity: Low. Action: confirm against the indenture.

- Cash flow lines with a dash or no printed figure are recorded as missing and not as zero: Cash paid for acquisitions, net of cash acquired (Q1 2026, H1 2026); Net proceeds from sale of senior notes (Q1 2025, H1 2025, Q1 2026); Equity contributions from noncontrolling interests (Q1 2025, H1 2025, 9M 2025, Q1 2026). This restricts those lines to the periods in which they are stated; the three activity totals and the cash roll-forward are unaffected. Severity: Low. Action: none needed.

- Discrete second-quarter and third-quarter 2026 cash flows: each quarterly report prints year-to-date cash flows only, so single-quarter cash flow figures are not stated; this restricts quarterly free cash flow to differences of printed totals. Severity: Low. Action: label any single-quarter cash flow as derived.

- Q4 2025 stand-alone figures: no fourth-quarter report or release was supplied, so the quarter is not stated; it would be the 2025 year less nine months 2025, both printed. This restricts any fourth-quarter comparison to a derived figure. Severity: Low. Action: label derived figures.

- Debt instrument terms: the Q3 report restates amounts but not the maturity dates, margins, commitments and amortisation of the Term Loans, the project loans and the UK facility, which are taken from the annual report at 2025-12-31; any amendment after that date other than the Virginia 3 refinancing, the Virginia 9 agreement and the securitization amendment is not reflected. Severity: Low. Action: confirm at the next report.

- Foreign currency debt: the euro notes, the Australian dollar term loan and the sterling facility are printed in US dollars at 2026-09-30, so their amounts in the currency of denomination at that date are not stated (the annual report states them at 2025-12-31); no exchange rate is used. Severity: Low. Action: none needed for carrying values.

- Rate basis of the Virginia 3 Term Loans due 2031, the benchmark and margin of the receivables securitization, and the scheduled amortisation of the project loans: not stated in the sources read; this restricts the floating-rate share of debt to the instruments whose rate basis is stated. Severity: Low. Action: obtain the loan terms.

- Post-balance-sheet effect of the dividend declared on 2026-11-05: the total amount is not stated (only 0.993 USD per share, record date 2026-12-15 and payment date 2027-01-06), so the effect on net debt, pro forma net debt and pro forma net leverage is not stated; the figure is not worked out here. Severity: Low. Action: state the amount when the issuer discloses the total.

- Operating KPIs: prior-year organic revenue growth, and data center leasing in the prior-year quarter and nine months, are not stated in the sources read; this restricts the dashboard to the current-year values for those rows. Severity: Low. Action: none needed.

spans.text: # Business & governance: IRON MOUNTAIN INC (irm), as of 2026-11-05
## Request

Business and governance for IRON MOUNTAIN INC (irm) as of 2026-11-05 on the credit snapshot pathway, a public-company case reported in USD. Scope: what the business is, who owns and governs it, how it earns money, which dated transactions shape it and where the seven supplied documents fall short; no transaction, sponsor deal or instrument recommendation is made.
## Sources

| EX-99.1_2026-08-05_final-q22026earningspres.htm.jsonl | Earnings press release (Exhibit 99.1) for the second quarter of 2026 | 2026-08-05 | 0d0d4258db90617a30c1e3c9ffb5f20e0de342df888db740df22d17b30f2e886 | Management commentary on data center leasing, dividend declaration |

## Findings
### Bottom line

Iron Mountain is a listed real estate investment trust with no sponsor or controlling holder named in the filings, so creditor risk comes from management's debt-funded data center build and rising dividend, not from sponsor extraction. Creditors get disclosure and covenants rather than control: the board sets dividends at its sole discretion, and the charter caps any one holder at 9.8% of the capital stock, subject to exceptions.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_irm-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 44; 10-K_2025-12-31_irm-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 45; 10-K_2025-12-31_irm-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 92; Source readiness (CP-0)

The operating base is steadier than the capital plan: storage contracts run one to five years and no customer exceeds about 3% of revenue, while data centers produced 50.44% of the nine-month rise in reportable-segment Adjusted EBITDA on 13.28% of revenue. That growth outruns internal cash: operating cash flow covered 69.81% of capital spending in the nine months to 30 September 2026, before USD 790.00 million of dividends, and net new senior-note proceeds of USD 1,485.00 million covered the USD 1,310.57 million left after dividends.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_irm-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-K_2025-12-31_irm-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 11; calculation CAL-28; calculation CAL-21; calculation CAL-35; calculation CAL-37; calculation CAL-38; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 6–7
### Key findings

No sponsor stands behind the credit and none is named above it, so the creditor-adverse behaviours to test are the board's own funding and payout choices, not a sponsor's leakage. The registrant is the top company of its own group, no preferred shares are in issue, and the filings name neither a parent nor a controlling holder; the holder list itself sits in a proxy statement that is not among the supplied documents, so control is not established beyond the charter cap. Creditors have no equity cure or parent support to rely on.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_irm-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 53; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 3; 10-K_2025-12-31_irm-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 92; 10-K_2025-12-31_irm-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 37; Source readiness (CP-0)

Reporting quality is sound and governance is conventional for a listed company, which supports monitoring but does not bind management. Both the annual statements and internal control carry unqualified audit opinions, each quarterly report is dated the same day as the matching earnings release, eleven directors signed the annual report including the chief executive, and the board oversees enterprise risk through a risk and safety committee. Director independence, the chair's role and director shareholdings are not established.

Dividend policy is the clearest creditor-adverse behaviour, because payouts rise while investment outruns operating cash flow. The quarterly dividend per share rose 10.06% in November 2025 and 14.93% in November 2026; in the nine months to 30 September 2026 the company paid USD 790.00 million of dividends while operating cash flow of USD 1,203.63 million covered 69.81% of capital spending of USD 1,724.21 million, and net senior-note proceeds of USD 1,485.00 million filled the gap. The real estate investment trust payout rule and a public pledge to grow dividends make the payout hard to cut, so it competes with debt reduction.

Basis: calculation CAL-34; calculation CAL-32; calculation CAL-33; calculation CAL-35; calculation CAL-38; calculation CAL-39; calculation CAL-40; 10-K_2025-12-31_irm-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 38; 10-K_2025-12-31_irm-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 45; 10-K_2025-12-31_irm-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 152; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 24; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 6–7

Growth capital is increasingly raised against single assets and with partners, which puts those lenders ahead of parent creditors on the assets concerned and shares the cash flows of the ventures with partners. At least four data center loans are secured on project subsidiaries' property or equity, including a new facility of up to USD 298.0 million signed in June 2026, and two partner-funded joint ventures added USD 124.70 million of noncontrolling interests. The parent notes are guaranteed only by U.S. subsidiaries holding the substantial majority of U.S. operations and are effectively subordinated to secured debt.

The records base is durable and the data center book is long-dated, but data center rent rolls over faster than the headline lease length suggests. Contracted storage runs one to five years with steady volumes, no customer is above about 3% of revenue, and data center leases average 10.3 years to expiry; even so, 27.24% of annualized data center rent expires in 2026 to 2028, and service growth in records and tape work is held back as stored records become less active.

Acquisition appetite is modest and revolver-funded, but the Regency Technologies earn-out is an identifiable cash call. Cash paid for acquisitions was USD 8.03 million in the nine months to 30 September 2026 against USD 101.63 million a year earlier, while the deferred purchase obligations, mostly that earn-out, rose to USD 210.19 million; an earn-out of up to USD 200.0 million would be payable in 2027 if earned. Redeemable noncontrolling interests of USD 62,186 thousand also carry put options on terms the documents do not state.

Basis: calculation CAL-47; calculation CAL-48; calculation CAL-45; calculation CAL-46; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 6; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 10; 10-K_2025-12-31_irm-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 134; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 10–11; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-K_2025-12-31_irm-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 117

Overall sponsor and governance risk reads as medium. Transparent reporting, no sponsor extraction, no liability management in the documents and covenant compliance sit against a debt-funded build, a rising payout, ring-fenced project debt and an ownership base the supplied documents cannot confirm.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 50; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 49; 10-K_2025-12-31_irm-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 53; 10-K_2025-12-31_irm-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 134; Source readiness (CP-0)
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against a medium reading is on the supportive side. Covenant ratios were well inside their limits at 30 September 2026 (net total lease adjusted leverage of 4.8x against a maximum of 7.0x, a headroom of 2.2x, and fixed charge coverage of 2.5x against a minimum of 1.5x, a headroom of 1.0x), the debt terms carry no rating trigger, no shares were repurchased in the latest quarter, maturities were extended through new notes, a refinanced project loan and a longer receivables programme with no waiver or covenant relief described, and the documents describe no priming, exchange offer or non-pro-rata transaction.

Against that, the dividend and the build could be more adverse than stated if the debt documents leave room for larger distributions, because the filings summarise covenants but do not show baskets. The view would turn adverse if the proxy statement showed a holder with board or veto rights, if the board funded a special distribution or buyback with debt while leverage sat near its limits, or if capital spending stayed above operating cash flow after leasing slowed. It would turn favourable if operating cash flow covered capital spending and dividends as the build tapers, or if executed debt documents showed tight restricted-payment limits.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 50; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 6–7; Source readiness (CP-0)
### Limitations

- Holder names, holder percentages and board independence are not in the supplied documents, so the conclusion that no holder controls the company rests on the charter cap and on the absence of any named holder, and stays provisional until a holder list is seen.

- The documents give no tenant-level detail for data centers beyond a statement that five of the largest hyperscalers are customers, so the durability of data center cash flow cannot be tested for tenant concentration.
- The 2026 acquisitions are not named or priced, so the conclusion on acquisition appetite rests on cash paid and goodwill acquired alone.

- The executed debt documents are not supplied, so whether dividend and investment baskets leave room for a larger distribution is not established and the dividend conclusion rests on observed payments rather than on legal capacity.

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

No sponsor buyout or change of control is described in the seven documents, and the latest acquisition with a disclosed price is Regency Technologies in January 2024, so there is no entry multiple or sources and uses to report for the period. The transactions that matter to creditors are financings, partner joint ventures, one finance lease and a small run of acquisitions.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_irm-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 133–134; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 6; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 10; Source readiness (CP-0)

New debt has been long-dated, with senior notes at the parent and secured project loans beside them. In September 2025 the company issued EUR 1,200.0 million of 4.75% senior notes due 2034 at par, and on 26 June 2026 it issued USD 1,500.0 million of 6.25% senior notes due 2035 at par, using net proceeds of USD 1,481.8 million to repay part of the revolving credit facility and for general corporate purposes. In January 2026 mortgage and mezzanine loans of USD 433.0 million due 2031 on the Virginia 3 data center replaced loans due in 2026, so the notes and the Virginia 3 loans together closed USD 1,933.00 million of term debt in 2026.

Other 2026 actions added capacity and extended maturities. The receivables securitisation programme was raised from USD 400.0 million to USD 450.0 million and extended from July 2027 to July 2029, with USD 408.0 million drawn at 30 September 2026. A new Virginia 9 credit agreement allows borrowing of up to USD 298.0 million at a margin of 3.00% over SOFR until June 2029, with USD 138.6 million drawn at the same date, and two joint ventures with partners added USD 124.70 million of noncontrolling interests.

Two items outside debt matter for cash. A 31-year data center finance lease signed in February 2026, with undiscounted minimum payments of about USD 223.4 million, is expected to start in the fourth quarter of 2026. On 5 November 2026, after the balance sheet date, the board declared a quarterly dividend 14.93% above the previous one, payable in January 2027.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Iron Mountain's fundamental credit is adequate but leverage-dependent: a contracted, diversified records base and a growing data center book support cash flow, yet net debt of 6.87x reported EBITDA, thin interest cover and negative free cash flow make credit quality depend on EBITDA outgrowing debt. Net debt over reported EBITDA fell from 7.88x at the end of 2025 to 6.87x at 30 September 2026 because earnings grew while debt rose; the dividend declared on 5 November 2026 is not reflected, and its pro forma effect on net debt is not established.

### Limitations
- No credit rating, agency report or peer set was supplied, so the adequate reading is a judgement on this issuer's own figures and not a ranking against comparable borrowers.

- Reported EBITDA is derived by Financial foundation while the company's guidance and several margin figures use its own Adjusted EBITDA, so every leverage conclusion carries two measures that differ by a gap that is not bridged line by line.

### Company description

Iron Mountain is a global information management group whose cash base is physical records storage and whose growth comes from data centers, digital solutions and asset lifecycle management. Global RIM Business produced 71.71% of nine-month 2026 revenue, Global Data Center Business 13.28% and Corporate and Other, which holds asset lifecycle management, 15.01%; storage rental was 56.73% of revenue and the United States 66.27% of FY2025 revenue, with other countries outside the United Kingdom and Canada 22.51%. The recurring, contracted rental base gives cash flow visibility and debt service capacity, while the service and asset lifecycle management lines add revenue that moves with activity and component prices.

### Ownership and group structure

Iron Mountain is a listed holding company with no sponsor, parent or controlling holder named; the charter caps any holder at 9.8% and the board sets dividends in its sole discretion, so creditors depend on governance and covenants rather than on a sponsor. Sponsor and governance risk is medium in Business & governance: reporting is transparent and covenants have headroom, but the payout is growing, project debt is ring-fenced and the proxy statement that would confirm holders is not among the supplied documents. The indentures treat a leveraged recapitalization as outside the change-of-control repurchase right, so the change-of-control put gives noteholders no protection against a debt-funded recapitalization.

### Revenue drivers and pricing power

Revenue is predictable in storage and data centers and cyclical or discretionary in service lines. Nine-month organic revenue growth was 15.6%, made up of storage rental at 11.6% and service at 21.3%; in Global RIM Business storage rental grew 5.4% organically on pricing with volume steady, while Global Data Center Business revenue grew 39.61% on lease commencements, pricing and power usage. Pricing power in records is therefore the base-business lever and carries the risk that price rises meet customer resistance as stored records become less active, whereas data center growth depends on leasing and energising capacity on schedule.

Service revenue and asset lifecycle management add volatility: Corporate and Other service revenue rose 61.0% in nine months partly through acquisitions and component pricing, buyers of decommissioned components are concentrated in China, and commodity prices move paper and scrap-metal sales. The unit's goodwill sensitivity is modest, with fair value 93.7% above carrying value at 1 October 2025, which limits near-term impairment risk but does not protect cash flow from a price fall.
### Cost structure and margin resilience

Margins are resilient on the consolidated measure and uneven underneath. Adjusted EBITDA margin was 36.7% in the nine months against 36.9% a year earlier; cost of sales rose to 46.6% of revenue from 44.6% as product cost of sales in asset lifecycle management went from 7.5% to 11.3% of revenue, offset by selling, general and administrative expense falling to 18.9% from 20.9%. Global RIM Business margin slipped to 43.7% from 44.4% while Global Data Center Business margin rose to 53.60%, so mix toward data centers supports margin and mix toward asset lifecycle management dilutes it; labor at 16.2% and facilities at 16.6% of revenue are treated here as largely fixed in the short run, which gives operating leverage on the way up and on the way down.
### Capital intensity and cash conversion

Capital intensity is high and almost all of it is discretionary growth spending. Last-twelve-months operating cash flow converted 58.99% of Adjusted EBITDA after cash interest took 31.68%, and in nine months growth investment was 93.07% of capital spending, of which 84.56% went to data centers; 2026 capital expenditure guidance is about USD 2,200.0 million of which USD 2,050.0 million is growth. Capital spending is flexible to the extent leases are not already committed, so the shortfall of USD 536.82 million over the last twelve months can narrow quickly if the company chooses, but customers who have preleased space in data centers under construction limit how fast.

### Competitive forces

Competitive pressure is moderate in records and higher in data centers and asset lifecycle management. In records most competitors operate in one market or region, so Iron Mountain's global scale and chain-of-custody record are a barrier that supports pricing; in data centers it competes with many developers on power availability, security, location, connectivity and rent, and in asset lifecycle management it competes with hyperscalers and corporate clients that process their own assets. New entrants face high capital and power barriers in data centers and trust barriers in records, which protects existing cash flows but also means the company must keep spending to hold its position.

Substitutes and buyers are the main sources of pressure on the base business: customers who adopt non-paper storage or retain records for less time shrink the physical volume and shift revenue from predictable storage to volatile service, and some large-customer contracts carry no limit on liability. Supplier power is real in data centers, where power, construction contractors and permits drive cost and timing, and in asset lifecycle management, where component buyers are concentrated; the credit consequence is cost and delay risk on the capacity that debt is funding.
### Macro, regulatory and technology factors

Interest rates, currency and tax rules matter to credit; political and social factors do not appear to be primary drivers in the supplied documents. Floating-rate debt and thin cover make rate changes material, 22.51% of FY2025 revenue arises outside the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada with euro and sterling debt acting as a partial natural hedge, a 10% depreciation of functional currencies would reduce equity by USD 374.7 million, and the real estate investment trust rules require a 90% distribution of taxable income, while a 2026 change in the limit on assets held in taxable subsidiaries and the global minimum tax are not expected to have a material effect. Digitisation and artificial intelligence cut both ways: they reduce physical record activity but support digital solutions.

### SWOT

Strengths are the contracted records base, long data center leases of 10.3 years on average and demonstrated market access; weaknesses are leverage of 6.87x reported EBITDA, a free cash flow shortfall of USD 536.82 million over the last twelve months and claims that rank ahead of parent noteholders. Opportunities that could improve credit quality are converting the data center development pipeline into leased rent and cross-selling, because only about 5% of customers buy from more than one business unit; threats that could weaken it are power and construction cost or delay, a faster shift away from physical records and higher refinancing cost.

### Financial profile and credit quality

Taking the nine dimensions in turn, scale and market position is strong, competitive advantage is average to strong in records and average in data centers and asset lifecycle management, business diversification is average because customers are diversified but 71.71% of revenue comes from one segment, cost and capex flexibility is average because growth spending is discretionary but partly committed, and margin stability is average to strong because the consolidated margin moved only 20 bp. Free cash flow stability is weak because the last twelve months left a shortfall of USD 536.82 million after capital expenditure, ability to refinance is average because access has been shown but 2027 maturities and floating-rate debt remain, liquidity is average at 1.95x cover of debt due within a year, and financial policy and governance is average because reporting is transparent and covenants have headroom while the payout is growing.

Basis: calculation CAL-42; calculation CAL-9; calculation CAL-13; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 42; 10-Q_2026-09-30_irm-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 50; Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A)

The main credit supports are the records base, data center EBITDA growth and market access; the main constraints are leverage, negative free cash flow and ranking. The trend is improving, with net debt over reported EBITDA at 6.87x against 7.88x and cash interest cover at 2.83x against 2.50x, but the improvement came from earnings and not from lower debt. Key missing datapoints are the debt maturity schedule after the 2026 refinancings, tenant concentration in data centers, covenant definitions and a rating.

### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

Over the next 12 to 24 months the outlook is supportive: management guides 2026 Adjusted EBITDA to USD 2,948 million to USD 2,978 million, a midpoint 15.11% above FY2025, has signed new data center leases this year, and says additional capacity is due to be energized over the next 24 months. Those are management statements and the rise in guidance is flattening, with the latest increase at the midpoint only USD 3.0 million. Tailwinds are lease commencements, pricing in records and falling restructuring cost; headwinds are higher power and construction cost, a rising dividend, rate-sensitive refinancing and records that are becoming less active.

Over three to five years the credit depends on converting the development pipeline into leased, cash-generating capacity while holding leverage steady: 27.24% of annualized data center rent expires in 2026 to 2028, which gives repricing opportunity but also re-leasing risk, and the 2027 and 2028 note maturities must be refinanced at current market cost. The records base is expected by management to stay relatively consistent in volume, so its contribution is stable cash rather than growth.

### Downside scenario

The primary downside path starts with a delay or shortfall in data center leasing or energizing while construction commitments continue, and turns into a leverage and refinancing problem rather than an immediate liquidity one. Revenue growth in the data center segment, now 39.61%, would slow first; because facility costs and the debt service on completed capacity would continue while rent was delayed, the segment margin of 53.60% would fall, and service and asset lifecycle management revenue would add to the pressure if component prices or activity weakened. As an arithmetic sensitivity and not a forecast, a 10% fall in last-twelve-months reported EBITDA with net debt and interest unchanged lifts net debt over reported EBITDA from 6.87x to 7.63x and cuts cash interest cover from 2.83x to 2.55x, close to the year-end 2025 levels of 7.88x and 2.50x, or to 6.84x and 2.84x on Adjusted EBITDA; a 1% rise in rates on uncovered floating-rate debt would add about USD 37.29 million of annual interest, 4.08% of cash interest, against the company's own year-end 2025 sensitivity of USD 41.9 million of net income for a 1% rise on 22.0% variable-rate debt.

Resilience appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress within a year: cash plus undrawn revolver of USD 2,406.38 million covers debt due within twelve months of USD 1,232.90 million 1.95x, the growth budget of USD 2,050.0 million can be reduced, partners contributed USD 95.17 million of equity in nine months, and covenant leverage of 4.8x sits 2.2x inside its 7.0x maximum. The levers are limited by the real estate investment trust distribution rule, which makes the dividend hard to cut, by minor asset-sale proceeds of USD 11.03 million, and by revolver availability that depends on the leverage test, so the exposure is to leverage staying near its current level while about 14.08% of year-end 2025 principal needs refinancing in 2027.

### Overall credit view

Overall, Iron Mountain presents an adequate business profile supported by a contracted, diversified records base and long-dated data center leases, but credit quality is constrained by net debt of 6.87x reported EBITDA, a free cash flow shortfall of USD 536.82 million over the last twelve months and claims that rank ahead of parent noteholders. Cash-flow durability appears adequate because maintenance spending and the dividend are self-funded and covenants have headroom, and refinancing capacity is likely to depend on continued EBITDA growth, the revolver and open bond markets, with about 14.08% of year-end 2025 principal due in 2027. The primary downside path is a data center slowdown that leaves debt-funded capacity idle while the payout keeps rising. Further analysis would require the maturity schedule after the 2026 refinancings, tenant concentration, the executed debt documents and a rating, and the dividend declared on 5 November 2026 is not reflected in the leverage figures, its pro forma effect on net debt not being established. The top risk is leverage that stays near its current level because EBITDA growth stalls.
